summary: A reflective, lyrical piece on foraging for and cooking with wild mushrooms, centered on autumn and the people who practice it. It profiles foragers, a mycologist and a chef, and covers the spiritual, seasonal, ethical, culinary and communal sides of the practice. It closes on foraging as a living tradition passed between generations.
one_line: A lyrical guide to autumn mushroom foraging and cooking, featuring foragers' voices on mindfulness, sustainability, seasonality and tradition.
key_facts: September 5th, 2023 marks the start of the foraging season for many fungi enthusiasts in the note.
Alice Martin is a seasoned forager who treats mushroom foraging as meditation and finds a cluster of earthy morels.
Autumn begins with the autumnal equinox on September 23rd, 2023, and is described as prime time for foragers, with cool nights and warm days.
Mycologist Dr. James Patterson says autumn brings 'a resurgence of life in fungal form'.
The fly agaric is described as a fairy tale classic with a red cap and white spots, while the chanterelle has golden hues and a refined taste.
Laura Thompson recalls October 14th as the date of her first successful hunt for the elusive porcini.
Michael Roberts, an advocate for ethical foraging, says: 'You take only what you need, and always leave the land as you found it.'
Sarah Kim goes to the woods on crisp December dawns and says foraging is about listening to what mushrooms tell you.
Chef Jacob Lee found a trove of oyster mushrooms on September 29th and made them the centerpiece of his autumnal menu.
Harold Greene finds peace while meticulously cleaning his harvest on an October afternoon, saying 'with each brush stroke, I find peace'.
Meals made with foraged mushrooms are described as a communion rooted in community and kinship.
The note presents foraging as a living tradition carried from one generation to the next, with foragers retreating once frost claims the fall's fungi.
